output.title: Decreasing students’ stress through time management training

scenes.narration: University students often feel stressed, and this paper asks whether a short time management training can lower that stress and raise control of time.
scenes.layout_description: A student sits beside a cluttered calendar while a small clock and highlighted arrows suggest a possible solution.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimalist hand-drawn student at desk with scattered papers, a clock, and orange/yellow arrows pointing toward a simple calendar, cream background, black ink line art.

scenes.narration: The authors studied twenty-three undergraduates who joined a training, then reported demands, perceived stress, and perceived control of time before and after.
scenes.layout_description: Three labeled measurement moments surround a small group of students in a simple loop.
scenes.visual_prompt: A small circle of 23 stick-figure students around three paper cards labeled before, 2 weeks, 4 weeks, with orange highlights on the timeline.

scenes.narration: They used a non-equivalent dependent variable design, meaning one variable should change with training, while demands should stay unchanged.
scenes.layout_description: Two paths split from one training box, one path changing and one staying flat.
scenes.visual_prompt: A training box sends one arrow to a rising line for stress and control, and another flat line for demands, with orange/yellow emphasis.

scenes.narration: The training focused on prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring, all presented as ways to manage study time better.
scenes.layout_description: Five small icons form a simple training sequence across the slide.
scenes.visual_prompt: A row of hand-drawn icons: priority list, target, stepping stones, daily schedule, checklist, with orange circles around the sequence.

scenes.narration: Students reflected on current activities, set concrete goals, planned steps, and thought about obstacles and deadlines for reaching those goals.
scenes.layout_description: A student looks at a list of activities beside a target and a small deadline marker.
scenes.visual_prompt: Student figure with thought bubble showing tasks, target, and a tiny flag marking a deadline, all in sparse line art.

scenes.narration: Next, they made daily schedules, deciding what to do, when and where to do it, and how to avoid distractions.
scenes.layout_description: A simple day planner sits beside a student pointing to time blocks and a crossed-out distraction icon.
scenes.visual_prompt: Open planner page with time blocks, a student figure, and a small crossed-out buzzing phone-like distraction symbol, orange accents on key blocks.

scenes.narration: The sample came from a medium-sized German university, with students from all faculties invited as an extracurricular activity without incentives.
scenes.layout_description: A campus building anchors a small invitation scene with students approaching from different directions.
scenes.visual_prompt: Minimal campus building with diverse student figures and invitation boards, cream background, black ink, orange arrows toward the training room.

scenes.narration: The training lasted 4 h, and questionnaires were filled in directly before training, then 2 weeks later, and again 4 weeks later.
scenes.layout_description: A straight timeline shows three questionnaire points and one training block in the middle.
scenes.visual_prompt: Horizontal timeline with a central 4 h block and three paper questionnaires at before, 2 weeks, and 4 weeks, highlighted in yellow.

scenes.narration: Of the 48 students who began, 27 completed the first follow-up and 23 completed all questionnaires, which were used for main analyses.
scenes.layout_description: A simple funnel narrows from the starting group to the analyzed group.
scenes.visual_prompt: A funnel-like visual of student icons shrinking from 48 to 27 to 23, with orange highlights on the final group.

scenes.narration: Those twenty-three students averaged 23.30 years old, and about half were female, studying subjects such as psychology, medicine, and law.
scenes.layout_description: A small cluster of students is surrounded by subject labels and a simple age note.
scenes.visual_prompt: Group of student figures with small handwritten subject labels around them and a tiny age tag, using sparse orange circles.

scenes.narration: Before training, most students said they had no or little experience with time management strategies, while only one reported some more experience.
scenes.layout_description: A simple bar-like set of self-ratings shows most responses clustered at the low end.
scenes.visual_prompt: Hand-drawn response scale with many marks near no and little experience, one mark near some more, orange accent on the low end.

scenes.narration: Time management behaviour was measured with 18 items, perceived stress with the tension scale, perceived control of time with ten items, and demands as control.
scenes.layout_description: Four measurement cards are arranged neatly, with the stress card highlighted as tension.
scenes.visual_prompt: Four paper cards labeled by simple icons: checklist, tension, clock control, and demands, with orange/yellow emphasis on the tension card.

scenes.narration: At time 1, time management behaviour correlated positively with perceived control of time, and perceived control of time correlated negatively with stress and demands.
scenes.layout_description: A small correlation map shows arrows between four variables with plus and minus signs.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple network diagram of four circles connected by lines, orange plus and minus symbols marking the relationships.

scenes.narration: The taught strategies were used more after training, with a significant increase from before training to 4 weeks later, and a nearly significant increase after 2 weeks.
scenes.layout_description: A usage line rises across the three time points, with the middle rise marked as nearly significant.
scenes.visual_prompt: Line chart style drawing of strategy use rising from before to 2 weeks to 4 weeks, with orange upward arrows and a dotted note at 2 weeks.

scenes.narration: For perceived stress, the repeated-measures analysis showed a significant overall time effect and a significant decrease 2 weeks after training.
scenes.layout_description: A stress gauge drops from the first to the second time point, with the effect marked clearly.
scenes.visual_prompt: A simple gauge labeled stress with the needle moving downward from before to 2 weeks, orange highlight around the lower reading.

scenes.narration: Perceived control of time showed only a tendency after 2 weeks, but by 4 weeks it had increased significantly compared with pretest.
scenes.layout_description: A clock icon rises slowly at first, then more clearly by the final time point.
scenes.visual_prompt: Three small clock symbols across a timeline, the first two modest, the last higher and circled in orange to show significance.

scenes.narration: At 4 weeks, both perceived stress and perceived control of time changed significantly, showing less stress and more control than before training.
scenes.layout_description: Two side-by-side arrows point in opposite directions from the pretest to the final measurement.
scenes.visual_prompt: Split panel with a downward stress arrow and upward control-of-time arrow, both highlighted in yellow and orange.

scenes.narration: The control variable demands did not change significantly at either follow-up, which matched the authors’ expectation for an unaffected measure.
scenes.layout_description: A flat line for demands sits beside the changing outcome lines.
scenes.visual_prompt: Flat horizontal line labeled demands across the three time points, with a small orange check mark beside it.

scenes.narration: Students with no or little prior experience seemed to benefit more, especially for perceived stress, than those with moderate or some experience.
scenes.layout_description: Two student groups are shown, with the less experienced group receiving larger highlighted arrows.
scenes.visual_prompt: Two clusters of students, one labeled less experience with bigger orange arrows to stress and control changes, the other with smaller arrows.

scenes.narration: The authors interpret the pattern as support for their idea that training can reduce perceived stress and increase perceived control of time.
scenes.layout_description: An interpretation bubble connects the training scene to the outcome scene.
scenes.visual_prompt: Training box leading to two outcome icons, stress down and control up, with a speech bubble-like note from the authors.

scenes.narration: They suggest prioritizing, goal setting, daily planning, and monitoring may give students more orientation and make goal-directed action easier.
scenes.layout_description: A student moves through a simple sequence of steps toward a goal flag.
scenes.visual_prompt: Step-by-step path from list to target flag, with small icons for planning and monitoring, orange path markers.

scenes.narration: The study also notes limitations: the sample was small, about half left before the second measurement, and larger studies are needed.
scenes.layout_description: The participant funnel reappears, now with a warning note beside the smallest group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Funnel of students with a small caution symbol and a note about needing larger studies, minimal orange accents.

scenes.narration: Because the intervention was homogeneous, the authors say it is clearer which training content may have produced the reported effects.
scenes.layout_description: A single clean training path is shown instead of many mixed components.
scenes.visual_prompt: One simple training path with consistent icons, contrasted with crossed-out extra components, orange circle emphasizing clarity.

scenes.narration: They argue that future research should compare time management training with other stress-reduction interventions and test whether effects persist.
scenes.layout_description: Two different intervention paths branch from a common starting point toward a follow-up point.
scenes.visual_prompt: Branching paths from one student to two different intervention boxes, then to a follow-up clock, with yellow highlights.

scenes.narration: The paper also points to possible performance outcomes, but says experimental studies are still needed to examine causal effects in higher education.
scenes.layout_description: A small performance chart sits beside a question mark and an experiment icon.
scenes.visual_prompt: Simple upward chart next to a lab-like experiment symbol and question mark, orange accent on the chart line.

scenes.narration: For students, the practical advice is simple: prioritize tasks, set clear goals with deadlines, plan the day, and monitor progress.
scenes.layout_description: A compact checklist fills the center, with each item marked by a small icon.
scenes.visual_prompt: Checklist with four illustrated items and orange check marks, clean and minimalist on cream background.

scenes.narration: Overall, this study suggests that a short time management training may help undergraduates feel less stressed and more in control of their time.
scenes.layout_description: A closing summary shows a student standing between a lower stress symbol and a higher control clock.
scenes.visual_prompt: Final balanced composition with one student, a lowered stress cloud on one side and an elevated clock on the other, orange and yellow highlights.
